evidence.excerpt:
We collected user queries from a deployed financial
deep research service during February to March
2026, applying standard privacy protection proce-
dures including anonymization and PII removal.
Query analysis revealed seven dominant categories:
Stock Comparison,Stock Trend Prediction,Funda-
mental Consultation,Stock Trading Advice,The-
me/Sector Analysis,Precious Metals Analysis, and
Individual Stock Analysis. Using stratified random
sampling across these categories, we constructed
a final dataset of 104 queries balancing analytical
complexity, temporal diversity, and entity cover-
age. Figure 2 shows the distribution of user queries
across fine-grained categories.

evidence.excerpt:
Our goal is not to keep human experts in the large-
scale execution loop, but to use human judgments
once to validate an automated rubric-screening
mechanism. We therefore compare three human
experts with a three-LLM judge panel on a sampled
subset of rubric items. This validation stage sup-
ports the operational claim needed by our pipeline:
in this benchmark setting, LLM-based rubric evalu-
ation is sufficiently aligned with human evaluation
to replace expert execution for large-scale screen-
ing.

After validation, we use the same three-LLM judge
panel to evaluate the full candidate pool. For a fixed
rubric under a fixed query, each of the 10 product
reports receives three binary judgments. A rubric
passes the consistency filter only if all three judges
agree on every one of the 10 reports. This strict
unanimity rule removes rubrics whose execution is
not sufficiently objective or reproducible.

evidence.excerpt:
Consistency alone is insufficient: a rubric may be
perfectly stable while still assigning the same effec-
tive judgment to all products. We therefore apply
a second filter at the cross-report level. For each
consistency-passed rubric, we compute the major-
ity label for each of the 10 product reports. A rubric
is considered distinguishable if at least one report
receives a majority-yes label and at least one re-
port receives a majority-no label. This removes
one-sided rubrics such as always-yes or always-no
criteria that are stable but uninformative for product
comparison.

We evaluate 10 commercial deep research products
in total using both the 3,687 consistency-passed
rubrics and the final set of 2,600 consensus-derived
gold rubrics obtained after distinguishability filter-
ing. Table 3 reports the nine published products,
while one held-out Internal System is described
separately in the text. For each rubric set, we re-
port two complementary metrics: Item-level Pass
Rate, defined as the proportion of rubrics on which
the product receives a positive label; and Query-
level Macro Pass Rate, defined by first comput-
ing the pass rate within each query and then av-
eraging across the 104 queries with equal weight.
The former reflects aggregate performance over the
retained rubric pool, while the latter controls for
query-level imbalance in rubric counts.

More broadly, our results suggest that rubric-
based evaluation for deep research can move be-
yond small, manually curated expert pipelines to-
ward a scalable alternative: generate a large can-
didate pool, validate LLM evaluation against hu-
man judgments, and derive high-quality rubrics
through consistency and distinguishability filtering.
Because this framework removes human-expert
execution from the critical path, it is naturally
suited to benchmark evaluation, automatic system
comparison, and future work on evaluation-driven
improvement of deep research systems. Impor-
tant limitations remain, including temporal sen-
sitivity of financial data, domain specificity, and
product-version drift. Future work includes extend-

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Claims regarding the scalability, expert-free final execution, and discriminative capacity of consensus-derived gold rubrics are directly supported by statistical filtering results, inter-annotator agreement metrics, and stable system rankings across diverse splits.
primary.evaluation_assessment: The empirical evaluation thoroughly validates batched judge stability, measures high human-LLM label agreement (98.67% on jointly unanimous items, Cohen's kappa 0.9733), demonstrates clear system separation across 10 commercial systems, and provides robust sensitivity checks including leave-one-judge-out and split-half distinguishability ablations.
primary.limitations: The authors explicitly note limitations regarding temporal sensitivity of financial domain data, rapid product version drift, and the need for future validation across other specialized professional domains.
primary.method_assessment: The methodology is clearly specified: candidate rubrics synthesized for 104 real-world financial queries across 1,040 reports are evaluated by a panel of three LLM judges, validated against three human financial analysts on 4,052 instances, and filtered through strict cross-judge unanimity and cross-system distinguishability.
primary.quality_rationale: The manuscript establishes an ecologically grounded, technically rigorous evaluation framework with sound controls, explicit inter-rater agreement analyses, and comprehensive sensitivity checks supporting all core claims.
primary.scoped_contribution: FinResearchBench II presents a pipeline for benchmarking deep research financial reports by synthesizing query-specific candidate rubrics from generated reports and filtering them via multi-LLM consensus (strict unanimity and distinguishability) after human-expert validation.

scholarly_quality.rationale: The manuscript establishes an ecologically grounded, technically rigorous evaluation framework with sound controls, explicit inter-rater agreement analyses, and comprehensive sensitivity checks supporting all core claims.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The authors explicitly note limitations regarding temporal sensitivity of financial domain data, rapid product version drift, and the need for future validation across other specialized professional domains.
